steps.say: In the last page we saw the monochromatize function that solves the chameleons problem using a function. Now this final page is the chapter summary. Let us revise every key idea, because these are very important for the board exam.

First, algorithms are carried out using the statements of a programming language. When some statements must be repeated many times, we put them in a subroutine. A subroutine is a small part of a program used again and again for one particular task. In programming languages, subroutines are called functions.

board.title: Subroutine
board.body: Small part of a program used repeatedly for a particular task

board.title: Function
board.body: A unit of code, usually defined within a bigger program

steps.say: A function works on many kinds of inputs, like variables and expressions, and gives a consistent output. Also remember that definitions have distinct syntax blocks. A definition binds a value to a name. It is not an expression.

board.title: Definition binds a value to a name; it is not an expression

steps.say: Next, parameters and arguments. Parameters are the variables in the function definition. Arguments are the values passed to the function definition. When we write type annotations in a function definition, the brackets are compulsory. This is a favourite one mark question.

board.title: Arguments
board.body: Values passed to the function definition

steps.say: Now interface and implementation. An interface is the set of actions an object can do. It defines the actions, but does not actually perform them. Implementation carries out the instructions defined in the interface. Think of the accelerator of a car. The pedal is the interface. The engine working inside is the implementation.

board.title: Interface
board.body: Set of actions an object can do; only defines them

board.title: Implementation
board.body: Carries out the instructions defined in the interface

steps.say: Finally, pure and impure functions. A pure function gives the same answer whenever the same arguments are passed, and it has no side effects. An example is sin of zero, or the square function. A function that has side effects, even without parameters, is an impure function. Examples are random and date. Changing a variable outside the function is a side effect.

board.title: Pure function
board.body: Same arguments, same result; no side effects

board.title: Impure function
board.body: Has side effects; result may differ, e.g. random(), date()

steps.say: Well done! If you remember these points, you can answer the two mark, three mark and five mark questions of this chapter confidently.

explainAgain.say: Think of a function like a tuition teacher's fixed method for solving one type of sum. You give the numbers, and the method gives you the answer. You can use the same method again and again, so you do not rewrite the steps each time.

board.title: Function = reusable method for one task

explainAgain.say: Parameters are the empty boxes written in the question paper. Arguments are the actual numbers you fill in. An interface is like the buttons on a calculator. Implementation is the circuit inside that does the work.

board.title: Parameter = empty box; Argument = value filled in

explainAgain.say: A pure function is like a vending machine with a fixed price. Same coin, same biscuit, every time. An impure function is like a lucky draw. The same ticket may give a different result each time.

board.title: Pure = predictable; Impure = unpredictable or changes outside things

example.say: Let us decide whether two functions are pure or impure. The first function, square, returns x times x. The second function, inc, adds x to an outside variable y and returns y. Square gives the same output for the same input, so it is pure. Inc changes the outside variable y, so the answer changes every call. So inc is impure, and its side effect is changing y.

board.title: Pure: square
board.body:
let square x:=
 return: x * x

board.title: Impure: inc

checkQuestion.question: What is the difference between a pure function and an impure function?
checkQuestion.idealAnswer: A pure function always returns the same result for the same arguments and has no side effects, for example square or sin of zero. An impure function may give different results for the same arguments or change outside variables, so it has side effects, for example random or date.
